Text: In a transcription unit, upstream sequences precede and downstream sequences follow one reference point: the {{c1::transcript initiation site}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the transcript initiation site is designated +1 and corresponds to the first (5′) nucleotide of the RNA transcript; base pairs before it carry minus (−) prefixes, and those after it, counted in the direction of transcription, carry plus (+) prefixes.

Ex: the −35 and −10 elements of an E. coli promoter are upstream sequences, with midpoints about 35 and 10 base pairs before the initiation site.

Thus they are called the −10 sequence and the −35 sequence, respectively.'

Text:
In an E. coli promoter, the two conserved consensus sequences, as read on the {{c2::nontemplate::template or nontemplate}} strand, are:

−10 sequence → {{c1::TATAAT::sequence}}

−35 sequence → {{c1::TTGACA::sequence}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: a consensus sequence is the nucleotide sequence found most often in a conserved element; individual promoters vary slightly from it, and hundreds of sequenced E. coli promoters otherwise have surprisingly little in common.

Why: the −10 sequence is AT-rich, and that is what lets the DNA unwind locally there, an essential prerequisite to synthesizing a new RNA chain.

Cue: the two elements are named for their midpoints, about 10 and 35 base pairs before the +1 initiation site, and the spacing between them is highly conserved at 15 to 20 base pairs.
verified_against: p282: 'The −10 consensus sequence in the nontemplate strand is TATAAT; the −35 consensus sequence is TTGACA.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p282: 'Hundreds of E. coli promoters have been sequenced and found to have surprisingly little in common. Two short sequences within these promoters are sufficiently conserved to be recognized, but even these are seldom identical in two different promoters.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p282: 'Although these sequences vary slightly from gene to gene, some nucleotides are highly conserved. The nucleotide sequences that are present in such conserved genetic elements most often are called consensus sequences.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p282: 'The AT-rich −10 sequence facilitates the localized unwinding of DNA, which is an essential prerequisite to the synthesis of a new RNA chain.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p282: 'The midpoints of the two conserved sequences occur at about 10 and 35 nucleotide pairs before the transcription-initiation site (Figure 11.8). Thus they are called the −10 sequence and the −35 sequence, respectively.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p282: 'The distance between the −35 and −10 sequences is highly conserved in E. coli promoters, never being less than 15 or more than 20 nucleotide pairs in length.'

Text: In an E. coli promoter, the sigma subunit of RNA polymerase initially binds the {{c1::−35::−10 or −35}} sequence, which is therefore sometimes called the {{c2::recognition}} sequence.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the other conserved element, the AT-rich −10 sequence, is where RNA polymerase initiates the localized unwinding of the DNA strands, not where sigma first binds.

Why: sigma is the subunit that mediates RNA polymerase's binding to promoters; a core enzyme with no sigma starts RNA chains at random sites on both strands of DNA.

Pathway: sigma binds the −35 → RNA polymerase unwinds the DNA at the AT-rich −10 → transcription begins within the transcription bubble, five to nine base pairs beyond the −10.

Text:
E. coli has two types of transcription terminator, classified by whether termination needs a protein called {{c1::rho (ρ)}}:

{{c1::rho-dependent}} terminators end transcription only in the presence of that protein

{{c1::rho-independent}} terminators end transcription without that protein
Back Extra:
Distinguish: both terminator types make RNA polymerase pause at an RNA hairpin; a rho-dependent terminator adds a 50–90 base-pair C-rich, G-poor stretch upstream of the inverted repeats (a stretch whose RNA forms no hairpin) and a rut (rho utilization) site near the 3′ end of the transcript.

Mechanism: rho binds the rut sequence of the transcript, travels 5′ to 3′ behind RNA polymerase, catches up while the polymerase is paused at the hairpin, and unwinds the DNA/RNA pairing with its helicase activity to release the transcript.

Meaning: termination begins when RNA polymerase encounters a termination signal; the transcription complex then dissociates and releases the nascent RNA.
verified_against: p283 (rendered page; text layer did not locate this mark): 'One type results in termination only in the presence of a protein called rho (ρ); therefore, such termination sequences are called rho-dependent terminators. The other type results in the termination of transcription without the involvement of rho; such sequences are called rho-independent terminators.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p283: 'Termination of RNA chains occurs when RNA polymerase encounters a termination signal. When it does, the transcription complex dissociates, releasing the nascent RNA molecule. There are two types of transcription terminators in E. coli.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p284: 'The mechanism by which rho-dependent termination of transcription occurs is similar to that of rho-independent termination in that both involve the formation of a hydrogen-bonded hairpin structure upstream from the site of termination. In both cases, these hairpins impede the movement of RNA polymerase, causing it to pause.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p284: 'However, rho-dependent terminators contain two additional sequences: a 50–90 nucleotide-pair sequence upstream from the inverted repeat sequences that produces an RNA strand with many C's but few G's, which therefore forms no hairpins or other secondary structures, and a sequence specifying a rho protein binding site called rut (for rho utilization) near the 3′ end of the transcript.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p284: 'Rho protein binds to the rut sequence in the transcript and moves 5′ to 3′ following RNA polymerase. When polymerase encounters the hairpin, it pauses, allowing rho to catch up, pass through the hairpin, and use its helicase activity to unwind the DNA/RNA base-pairing at the terminus and release the RNA transcript.'

Text: In rho-independent termination in E. coli, the terminator's GC-rich {{c1::inverted repeats::DNA sequence feature}} are transcribed → the RNA copied from them folds into a {{c1::hairpin::RNA structure}} immediately after those regions are synthesized → the folded RNA makes RNA polymerase {{c1::pause::effect on the enzyme}} in chain extension.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: inverted repeats are sequences in each DNA strand that are inverted and complementary, so the single-stranded RNA transcribed from them is self-complementary and base-pairs with itself into the hairpin.

Distinguish: a rho-dependent terminator also forms a hairpin that pauses RNA polymerase; there the transcript is freed by rho, which catches the paused polymerase and unwinds the DNA/RNA pairing with its helicase activity.

Pitfall: the hairpin forms in the RNA transcript, not in the DNA; the DNA only carries the inverted repeats that encode it.
verified_against: p283 (rendered page; text layer did not locate this mark): 'When transcribed, these inverted repeat regions produce single-stranded RNA sequences that can base-pair and form hairpin structures (Figure 11.10, bottom). The RNA hairpin structures form immediately after the synthesis of the participating regions of the RNA chain and retard the movement of RNA polymerase molecules along the DNA, causing pauses in chain extension.' | stem context (unmarked, not clozed) p283: 'Rho-independent terminators contain a GC-rich region followed by six or more AT base pairs, with the A's present in the template strand (Figure 11.10, top). The nucleotide sequence of the GC-rich region contains inverted repeats—sequences of nucleotides in each DNA strand that are inverted and complementary.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p284: 'The mechanism by which rho-dependent termination of transcription occurs is similar to that of rho-independent termination in that both involve the formation of a hydrogen-bonded hairpin structure upstream from the site of termination. In both cases, these hairpins impede the movement of RNA polymerase, causing it to pause.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p284: 'When polymerase encounters the hairpin, it pauses, allowing rho to catch up, pass through the hairpin, and use its helicase activity to unwind the DNA/RNA base-pairing at the terminus and release the RNA transcript.'

Text: In {{c2::rho-independent::rho-dependent or rho-independent}} termination in E. coli, once the RNA hairpin has made RNA polymerase pause, the run of {{c1::U's::nucleotide}} that {{c1::follows::precedes or follows}} the hairpin region facilitates release of the newly made RNA from the DNA template.
Back Extra:
Why: AU base-pairing is the weakest of the standard base pairs, needing the least energy to separate, so the U's paired with the template's A's let go while RNA polymerase sits stalled at the hairpin.

Mechanism: a rho-independent terminator is a GC-rich region followed by six or more AT base pairs with the A's in the template strand, so the transcript carries the hairpin and then the run of U's.

Distinguish: at a rho-dependent terminator the paused polymerase is instead caught by rho, which unwinds the DNA/RNA pairing with its helicase activity to free the transcript.

Text: In {{c1::prokaryotes::prokaryotes or eukaryotes}}, the {{c2::transcription}}, {{c2::translation}}, and {{c2::degradation}} of an mRNA molecule often occur {{c1::simultaneously::simultaneously or sequentially}}.
Back Extra:
Why: an mRNA is synthesized, translated, and degraded all in the 5′ to 3′ direction, and in prokaryotes no nuclear envelope separates the ribosomes from the site of mRNA synthesis, so the 5′ end of a transcript serves as a template for polypeptide synthesis as soon as it is made.

Distinguish: in eukaryotes RNA is synthesized in the nucleus, and most protein-coding RNAs must be transported to the cytoplasm before ribosomes translate them.

Ex: Oscar Miller and Barbara Hamkalo visualized the coupling of transcription and translation in bacteria by electron microscopy: a single E. coli gene being transcribed into many mRNAs, each already loaded with the ribosomes translating it.

Since mRNA molecules are synthesized, translated, and degraded in the 5′ to 3′ direction, all three processes can occur simultaneously on the same RNA molecule.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p284: 'In prokaryotes, the polypeptide-synthesizing machinery is not separated by a nuclear envelope from the site of mRNA synthesis.
